anchor.quote: a recursion's cost per bit can grow as a fixed power of its parameter, with exponent $\lambda<1$
Let $f$ be the parameter of a call
Here $m$ is the factor by which the parameter grows
Let $s$ be the number of subcalls of one call.
Let $\Phi(f)$ be the cost of a call divided by the volume $V$ it works on.
Let $C$ be a constant such that the call's own outside work is at most $C(mf)^\lambda$
Here $\Omega$ is the bit count of one axis chunk
Let $\nu$ count the levels of unrolling

anchor.note: Big-O notation is covered by the reader profile (asymptotic analysis).
Logarithms to a base are covered by the undergraduate computer science profile.

gaps.quote: Each leaf is handled by one kernel per chunk
gaps.note: The reader is never told what a kernel is (in the paper, the individual selected-bit butterfly kernel C applied to one axis chunk, costing O(V) per kernel, paper lines 2208-2225) nor what a chunk is, so the leaf cost O(f/m^nu) cannot be checked.

gaps.quote: A row addition on fields of $u=f\Omega$ bits costs $O(V(u^\tau+1))$.
gaps.note: The page gives no reason why a row addition costs this much, and its only cited bound is for an address interchange. In the paper (lines 2226 and 2295-2298) this bound comes from the packed-selected-bit-rectangle lemma, for a row addition on f selected bits (one per K-bit chunk) of whole slots, under that lemma's asymptotic hypotheses, not for adding two u-bit fields. The reader also cannot see why the outside work is only a fixed number of such additions.

gaps.quote: Taking $\lambda$ with $\log_m(s/W)<\lambda<1$ makes the ratio below 1
gaps.note: The choice of lambda also has to satisfy lambda > tau(1+eta/vartheta) from the outside-work bound, and lambda > tau, sigma. That is possible only if eta is small enough that tau(1+eta/vartheta)<1; the page says only that eta>0 is fixed. The paper (lines 2394-2399) requires max{tau,sigma}<lambda<1 and tau(1+c/beta)<lambda, so the page is missing the hypothesis on eta and the full list of conditions on lambda.

The inequality does not follow and is false in general. Since f can be as small as d^vartheta, f^sigma d^{vartheta(1-sigma)} can equal f, which exceeds f^lambda. The paper (lines 2423-2426) stops at O(e^sigma d^{beta(1-sigma)}) and in its final bound (lines 2437-2444) keeps the separate term d^{sigma+beta(1-sigma)}, which forces the weaker exponent lambda' > max{lambda, sigma+beta(1-sigma)}, not lambda.

gaps.quote: The leaves at depth $\nu$ have $u=f/m^\nu<d^\vartheta$ chunks
gaps.note: Here u is a number of chunks, but earlier on the same page u is a bit width (address fields of u bits, and u=f Omega bits) and no change of meaning is announced. Reading u as a bit count would make u^tau and the leaf cost inconsistent.

gaps.quote: each on a stream of volume $V/W$
gaps.note: The exact volume V/W requires the stream to be split into W role streams by a row field whose length is divisible by W^k (paper lines 1481-1483, 2316-2321). The page states no row hypothesis, and gives no reason why the parameter must be a power of m, so the claim is stated without a hypothesis it needs.
